[[File:Quercus Suber (wrinkled skin).jpg|thumb|Bark of tree 'wrinkled skin']]
'''''Quercus suber''''', commonly called the '''cork oak''', is a medium-sized, [[evergreen]] [[oak]] tree in the section [[Quercus sect. Cerris|''Quercus'' sect. ''Cerris'']]. It is the primary source of [[cork (material)|cork]] for wine bottle stoppers and other uses, such as cork flooring and as the cores of [[cricket ball]]s.  It is native to southwest Europe and northwest [[Africa]]. In the [[Mediterranean basin]] the tree is an ancient species with [[fossil]] remnants dating back to the [[Tertiary period]].<ref>{{cite book|author=Eriksson, E.|author2=Varela, M.C.|author3=Lumaret, R.|author4=Gil, L.|name-list-style=amp|title=Genetic conservation of ''Quercus suber''|publisher=European Forest Genetic Resources Programme ([[EUFORGEN]]), [[Bioversity International]]|date=2017|isbn=978-92-9255-062-2|url=http://www.euforgen.org/fileadmin/templates/euforgen.org/upload/Publications/Thematic_publications/Quercus_TB_OpenSourceCR_web.pdf}}</ref> It can survive for as long as two centuries. Typically, once it reaches 25 years old, its thick bark can be harvested for cork every 9 to 12 years without causing harm to the tree.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cork Oak |url=https://www.rainforest-alliance.org/species/cork-oak/ |access-date=2024-04-28 |website=Rainforest Alliance |language=en-US}}</ref>

It endures drought and makes little demand on the [[soil quality]] and is regarded as a defence against [[desertification]]. Cork oak [[woodland]]s are home to a multitude of animal and plant species. Since cork for sealing bottles is increasingly being displaced by other materials, these forests are at risk as part of the cultural landscape and as a result animal species such as the [[Iberian lynx]] and [[Spanish imperial eagle|imperial eagles]] are threatened with extinction.<ref name="WWF">{{cite web |title=Put a cork in it! |url=https://wwf.panda.org/wwf_news/?4802/Put-a-cork-in-it |publisher=[[World Wildlife Fund|WWF]] |access-date=13 February 2021}}</ref>

==Description==
===General appearance and bark===

The cork oak grows as an [[evergreen]] tree, reaching an average height of {{Convert|10 to 15|m|abbr=off}} or in rare cases up to 25 m and a trunk diameter ([[Diameter at breast height|DBH]]) of {{convert|50|to|100|cm|abbr=off}}. It forms a dense and asymmetrical crown that starts at a height of {{Convert|2–3|m|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}} and spreads widely in free-standing trees. The crown can be divided into several separate, rounded partial crowns.<ref name="page501">{{cite book |vauthors=Schütt et al. |title= Enzyklopädie der Laubbäume. Page 501}}</ref><ref name="iberica">{{cite web |title=''Quercus suber'' L. |url=http://www.floraiberica.es/floraiberica/texto/pdfs/02_041_03_Quercus.pdf |publisher=[[Flora Iberica]] |access-date=14 February 2021}}</ref>

The young twigs are densely hairy light gray or whitish. Older branches are strong and knotty. Older trees only form short shoots between {{convert|7|and|15|cm|abbr=on|frac=2}} in length.<ref name="page501" />

The thick, longitudinally cracked cork layers of the gray-brown trunk bark are characteristic of the cork oak. The [[Cork cambium|cambium]] of the smooth bark of young trees forms a cork layer very early on, which can be {{convert|3|to|5|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} thick. The light and spongy cork fabric shows vertical cracks and is white on the outside and red to red-brown on the inside. After the cork has been harvested, the trunk appears reddish brown, but later it is significantly darker.<ref name="page501" /> The wood is ring-pored, has a brown heartwood and a light reddish sapwood.<ref name="page503">{{cite book |vauthors=Schütt et al. |title= Enzyklopädie der Laubbäume. Page 503}}</ref> The cork oak develops a taproot that reaches a depth of {{convert|1 to 2|m|ft|abbr=on|frac=4}} and from which several meters long, horizontally running side roots extend.<ref name="page502">{{cite book |vauthors=Schütt et al. |title= Enzyklopädie der Laubbäume. Page 502}}</ref> The trees can live over 400 years, and harvested specimens can be 150 to 200 years old.<ref name="page501" /><ref name="iberica" />

===Leaves===
[[File:Quercus suber - Köhler–s Medizinal-Pflanzen-254.jpg|thumb|Illustration from ''[[Köhler's Medicinal Plants]]'', 1887]]

The leathery [[leaves]] are alternate and are {{convert|2.5|to|10|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} long and {{convert|1.2|to|6.5|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} wide. The shape varies between round, oval and lanceolate-oval. The leaf blade has five to seven sharp teeth on both edges and a pointed vegetation cone (apex). The midrib stands out clearly on the underside of the leaf, the first-order lateral nerves usually lead to the teeth of the leaf margin. The upper side of the leaf is light green, the underside of the leaf whitish and densely hairy. There is no hair on young trees. The leaf stalks are {{convert|6|to|18|mm|frac=4}} long and are also hairy. At the base of the petiole are two narrow, lanceolate, {{convert|5|mm|abbr=on|frac=4}} long and bright red stipules that fall off in the first year. The new leaves appear in April and May, when older leaves are also shed. They usually stay on the tree for two to three years, less often only one year, the latter especially in severe environmental conditions and on the northern border of the distribution area. Extremely cold winters can also lead to complete defoliation.<ref name="page501" />

===Inflorescence and flower===
The cork oak is single sexed ([[monoecious]]), with both female and male flowers on one specimen.<ref name="page501" /> The female flowers form upright inflorescences in the leaf axils of young branches. These are formed from a hairy axis {{convert|5|to|30|mm|abbr=on|frac=4}} long with two to five separate flowers. The female flowers contain a small, hairy, four- to six-lobed [[Perianth|flower envelope]] and three to four [[Stigma (botany)#Style|styles]].<ref name="page502" /> The male [[catkin]]s also arise on the leaf axils of young branches. They are bright red at the beginning and stand upright, older catkins are yellow and pendulous, {{convert|4|to|7|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} long and have a whitish hairy axis. The single flowers are sessile and have a densely hairy flower cover that is colored red when opened. The four to six [[stamen]]s are whitish with yellow, egg-shaped anthers. They are longer than the bracts.<ref name="page501" />

===Infructescence, fruit and seed===
The [[Infructescence|fruit clusters]] are {{convert|0.5|to|4|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} long and carry two to eight acorns. About half of the fruits are enclosed in the fruit cup ([[Calybium and cupule|cupule]]); the fruit cups are {{convert|2|to|2.5|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} in diameter. The upper scales of the cupula are gray and hairy, in the subspecies ''Quercus suber occidentalis'' the scales are close together or are fused. The size of the acorns varies between lengths of {{convert|2|to|4.5|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} and diameters of {{convert|1|to|1.8|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}}. The fruit casing ([[pericarp]]) is bare, smooth and shiny brownish red. The [[Hilum (biology)|hilum]] (the starting point of the seed) is convex and has a diameter of {{convert|6|to|8|mm|abbr=on|frac=8}}.<ref name="page502" />

==Taxonomy==
''Quercus suber'' is a species of the section ''[[Quercus sect. Cerris|Cerris]]'' to which, for example, the following species also belong:
*[[Valonia oak]] (''Quercus macrolepis'')
*[[Quercus cerris|Turkey oak]] (''Quercus cerris'')
*''[[Quercus × crenata]]''
*[[Macedonian oak]] (''Quercus trojana'')

Characteristic for the section are the hairless [[pericarp]] and the usually two-year ripening time of the fruits. The cork oak is an exception because the fruits can ripen in both the first and the second year.<ref name="page500">{{cite book |vauthors=Schütt et al. |title= Enzyklopädie der Laubbäume. Page 500}}</ref>

In the species ''Quercus suber'' two subspecies are distinguished:

*''Quercus suber'' subsp. ''suber'': Nominal taxon
*''Quercus suber'' subsp. ''occidentalis''<small> (Gay) Bonnier & Layens</small>: It differs from the nominate form in the shape of the cupula scales, the longer development time of the fruits and the semi-evergreen foliage. The distribution area of the subspecies is the Portuguese Atlantic coast.<ref name="page500" />

Together with the Turkey oak (''Quercus cerris'') and the [[Quercus ilex|holm oak]] (''Quercus ilex''), the cork oak forms [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrids]].<ref name="page503" />

The scientific name ''Quercus suber'' is derived from the [[Latin]] word ''quercus'', which the Romans used to describe the [[pedunculate oak]] (''Quercus robur''). The [[specific name (botany)|specific epithet]] ''suber'' is Latin for cork oak, and also cork.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Genaust |first1=Helmut |title=Etymologisches Wörterbuch der botanischen Pflanzennamen |date=2005 |isbn=3-937872-16-7 |edition=3., vollständig überarbeitete und erweiterte Auflage |publisher=Nikol Verlagsgesellschaft |location=Hamburg |pages=523 and 618}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Alcornoques en Grazalema.jpg|thumb|right|Cork oak forest habitat]]
[[File:Cork oak trees near Roses Catalonia.jpg|thumb|Cork oak trees, near Roses, northeastern Spain]]
The cork oak occupies the area around the western [[Mediterranean basin]]. In Portugal, natural and cultivated stands cover an area of 750,000 hectares.<ref name="page500" /><ref name="APCOR" /> There are natural populations of the nominate form at altitudes between {{convert|150|and|300|m|abbr=on}} above sea level, the subspecies ''occidentalis'' is found along the [[Atlantic]] coast. In Spain the occurrences remain mostly below {{convert|600|m|abbr=on}}, but rarely reach heights of {{convert|1200|m|abbr=on}}. In Spain, cork oaks are common in the southern half of the country, as well as in the western and northeastern areas, but rare in central Spain. In Italy one finds natural occurrences along the [[Tyrrhenian Sea]] and in eastern [[Apulia]] on the [[Adriatic Sea]]. Also on the Adriatic is the cork oak on the [[Dalmatian coast]]. It is one of the most common forest trees in [[Sardinia]]. Natural and man-made occurrences exist in Africa on the Mediterranean coast of Tunisia, Algeria and [[Al-Maamora Forest|Morocco]] and at altitudes up to {{convert|1000|m|abbr=on}}, on the [[High Atlas]] up to {{convert|2000|m|abbr=on}}.<ref name="page500" /> In its native range, cork oak forests cover approximately {{convert|22000|sqkm|abbr=off}}.<ref name="iucn status 19 November 2021" /> Outside of its natural range, the cork oak is cultivated in the [[Crimea]], the [[Caucasus]], [[India]] and the [[Southwestern United States]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=J. Heller |title=''Quercus suber'' L. |url=http://mansfeld.ipk-gatersleben.de/apex/f?p=185:46:781663974789756::NO::module,mf_use,source,akzanz,rehm,akzname,taxid:mf,,botnam,0,,Quercus%20suber,17870 |publisher=Mansfeld's World Database of Agricultural and Horticultural Crops}}</ref> The subspecies ''Quercus suber occidentalis'' also thrives in mild areas of England.

The species needs a lot of light and cannot survive in dense populations. It loves warmth, grows at annual mean temperatures of {{convert|13|to|17|C}} and can withstand maximum temperatures of up to {{convert|40|C}}. In the area of distribution, the temperature rarely falls below freezing point, but temperatures down to {{convert|-5|C}} without damage and down to {{convert|-10|C}} without major damage can be tolerated. The cork oak is not hardy in [[Central Europe]]. It endures drought and survives dry periods in summer by reducing its metabolism. An annual rainfall of {{convert|500|to|700|mm}} is considered optimal, in cooler locations {{convert|400|to|450|mm}} can be sufficient with enough humidity. Cork oaks have low soil demands and also grow in poor, dry or rocky locations. They rarely thrive on [[limestone|calcareous]] soils, but they are often found on crystalline slates, on gneiss, granite and sands. The [[Soil pH|acidity of the soil]] should be between pH 4.5 and 7.<ref name="page504">{{cite book |vauthors=Schütt et al. |title= Enzyklopädie der Laubbäume. Page 504}}</ref>

The cork oak is considered a [[pyrophyte]] because it recovers quickly after forest fires as it is protected by the cork.{{cn|date=October 2023}}

==Ecology==
[[File:KorkeichePortugal1994.jpg|thumb|right|Cork oak [[savanna]]]]
[[File:Linces12.jpg|thumb|right|The [[Iberian lynx]], a resident of the cork oak forests of the southern [[Iberian Peninsula]]]]
The cork oak forest is one of the major plant communities of the [[Mediterranean woodlands and forests]] [[ecoregion]].<ref>[https://www.worldwildlife.org/ecoregions/pa1214 Mediterranean Woodland and Forest Ecoregion: Northern Africa: Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia.] World Wildlife Fund. 2017.</ref> In natural populations, the cork oak grows together with the holm oaks (''[[Quercus ilex]]'', ''[[Quercus rotundifolia]]''), the Portuguese oak (''[[Quercus faginea]]''), the Pyrenean oak (''[[Quercus pyrenaica]]''), Mirbeck's oak (''[[Quercus canariensis]]''), the maritime pine (''[[Pinus pinaster]]''), the stone pine (''[[Pinus pinea]]''), the strawberry tree (''[[Arbutus unedo]]'') and the olive tree (''[[Olea europaea]]''), in cooler locations also with the sweet chestnut (''[[Castanea sativa]]''). In addition to these tree species, the shrub-forming species include the Kermes oak (''[[Quercus coccifera]]''), the Lusitanian oak (''[[Quercus lusitanica]]'') the holly buckthorn (''[[Rhamnus alaternus]]''), species of the genus ''[[Phillyrea]]'', the myrtle (''[[Myrtus communis]]''), the green heather (''[[Erica scoparia]]''), the common smilax (''[[Smilax aspera]]'') and the Montpellier cistus (''[[Cistus monspeliensis]]'') are often found together with the cork oak.<ref name="page504" />

As a [[pyrophyte]], this tree has a thick, insulating bark that makes it well adapted to [[forest fire]]s.<ref name="iucn status 19 November 2021" /> After a fire, many tree species regenerate from seeds (as, for example, the [[maritime pine]]) or re-sprout from the base of the tree (as, for example, the [[Quercus rotundifolia|holm oak]]). The bark of the cork oak allows it to survive fires and then simply regrow branches to fill out the canopy. The quick regeneration of this oak makes it successful in the fire-adapted ecosystems of the [[Mediterranean climate|Mediterranean biome]].<ref name=santos>Santos Pereira, J., Bugalho, M.N., and Caldeira, M.D. (2008). [http://www.apcor.pt/wp-content/uploads/2015/09/From-the-Cork-Oak-to-Cork-a-sustainable-system.pdf ''From the Cork Oak to Cork: A Sustainable Ecosystem''.] APCOR: Portuguese Cork Association.</ref>

=== Symbiosis ===
[[File:Amanita caesarea.JPG|thumb|right|The Caesar's mushroom, a symbiotic partner of the cork oak]]
The cork oak enters into a [[mycorrhizal]] [[symbiosis]] with several types of [[fungus]]. The fine root system of the oak is in close contact with the mycelium of the fungus. The oak receives water and nutrient salts from the fungus in exchange for products of photosynthesis. Such a symbiosis exists among others with the following species:<ref name="page502" />

*[[Caesar's mushroom]] (''Amanita caesarea'')
*[[Death cap]] (''Amanita phalloides'')
*[[Panther cap]] (''Amanita pantherina'')
*[[Amanita gilbertii|Gilbert's limbed lepidella]] (''Amanita gilbertii'')
*[[Cep]] (''Boletus edulis'')
*''[[Russula rubra]]''

=== Diseases and predators ===

[[File:gypsy moth invasive moth caterpillar lymantria dispar.jpg|thumb|right|Spongy moth caterpillar]]

The most virulent cork oak pathogen may be ''[[Diplodia corticola]]'', a [[Ascomycota|sac fungus]] which causes sap-bleeding sunken canker wounds in the wood, withering of the leaves, and lesions on the acorns. The fungus ''[[Biscogniauxia mediterranea]]'' is becoming more common in cork oak forests. Its fruiting bodies appear as charcoal-black cankers. Both of these fungi are transmitted by the [[Platypus cylindrus|oak pinhole borer]] (''Platypus cylindrus''), a species of weevil.<ref name=mor/>

The common water mould ''[[Phytophthora cinnamomi]]'' grows in the roots of the tree and has been known to devastate cork oak woodlands.<ref name=mor/>

Several species of butterflies damage the cork oak, the most important being the [[Lymantria dispar|spongy moth]] (''Lymantria dispar''). The species lays its eggs in the bark of the branches and trunks, and the caterpillars that hatch in spring are distributed in the crown and eat them bare. The bacterial species ''[[Bacillus thuringiensis]]'' is used as a biological plant protection agent against the spongy moth. Another pest is the [[green oak tortrix]] (''Tortrix viridana''), whose caterpillars eat flowers and young leaves and roll them up with thread to form typical coils. The [[lackey moth]] (''Malacosoma neustria'') also causes damage to the leaves, sticking its eggs to the bark of thin twigs in multiple rows, and also the [[brown-tail moth]] (''Euproctis chrysorrhoea''), whose caterpillars skeletonize the leaves and further damage the tree after overwintering in spring. A special cork pest is the [[jewel beetle]] ''[[Coraebus undatus]]'', which lays its eggs in the cork tissue. Another harmful species of beetle is the [[great capricorn beetle]] (''Cerambyx cerdo''), whose larvae eat long corridors in the oak wood.<ref name="page504-505">{{cite book
 | pages    = 504–505
 | title    = Enzyklopädie der Laubbäume
 | vauthors = Schütt et al.
}}</ref>

Unfavorable climatic conditions and fungal attack are made responsible for the weakening of trees and for crown damage. Such fungal parasites of weakness are ''[[Botryosphaeria stevensii]]'', ''Biscogniauxia mediterranea'', ''[[Endothiella gyrosa]]'' and representatives of the mold genus ''[[Fusarium]]''. Drought and parasite infestation are also considered to be the cause of the weakness syndrome in parts of Spain and Portugal.<ref name="page504-505" />

[[File:Cork oak trunk section.jpg|thumb|right|A cross-section of the trunk, showing the thick spongy bark used for making wine bottle corks]]

The cork oak is grown for the production of cork in several Mediterranean countries. The centers of cork production are in southern Portugal (accounting for 50% of the total production<ref name="APCOR">{{cite web |title=Information Bureau: 2019 Cork Sector in Numbers - APCOR |url=http://www.apcor.pt/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/CORK-SECTOR-IN-NUMBERS_EN.pdf |publisher=APCOR |access-date=13 February 2021}}</ref>) and southern Spain, where low trees with large crowns and strong branches are grown in large areas, which provide the highest yield of cork.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Schütt |first1=Schuck |title=Lexikon der Baum- und Straucharten: das Standardwerk der Forstbotanik. Morphologie, Pathologie, Ökologie und Systematik wichtiger Baum- und Straucharten |date=2002 |publisher=Nikol Verl.-Ges |location=Hamburg |isbn=3-933203-53-8 |page=436 |edition=Sonderausg}}</ref> These mostly extensively managed habitats are called ''[[dehesa|montados]]'' in Portugal and ''[[dehesa]]s'' in Spain.<ref name='gil08'>{{citation |author=Gil, L. |author2=Varela, M. |name-list-style=amp|title=Cork oak - ''Quercus suber'': Technical guidelines for genetic conservation and use|date=2008 |page=6 |url=http://www.euforgen.org/fileadmin//bioversity/publications/pdfs/1323_Cork_oak__Quercus_suber_.pdf |publisher=[[European Forest Genetic Resources Programme]]}}</ref> They are considered to be extremely valuable from the point of view of biodiversity and cultural heritage.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Plieninger |first1=Tobias |title=Traditional land-use and nature conservation in rural Europe |url=https://editors.eol.org/eoearth/wiki/Traditional_land-use_and_nature_conservation_in_rural_Europe |publisher=[[Encyclopedia of Earth]]}}</ref>

The cork consists of dead, air-filled, thin-walled cells and contains [[cellulose]] and [[suberin]]. Cork is heat and sound insulating, the suberine gives it water-repellent properties. The cork layer is replicated by the cork-producing [[Cork cambium|phellogen]] and can therefore be harvested repeatedly without damaging the tree too much. The first harvest usually takes place after about 25 years with a trunk diameter (DBH) of {{convert|70|cm|abbr=on}}, though new techniques (such as better irrigation systems) could shorten it to only 8 to 10 years.<ref name="Amorim">{{cite web |title=Mitos e curiosidades |url=https://www.amorim.com/a-cortica/mitos-e-curiosidades/Quanto-tempo-vive-um-sobreiro/110/400/ |publisher=[[Corticeira Amorim|Amorim]] |access-date=13 February 2021}}</ref><ref name="iucn status 19 November 2021" /> The first cork layer is called "male cork" or "virgin cork", is still not very elastic and cracked and is only used for insulating mats. The second harvested cork (known as ''secundeira''), has a more regular structure and is softer, but is still only used for insulation and in decorative objects.<ref name="Amorim" /> Only the following cork harvests deliver a higher quality cork, the "female cork", which can be used commercially in full. The best quality cork is obtained from the third and fourth harvest. Cork harvesting takes place every nine to twelve years when a layer thickness of {{convert|2.7|to|4|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} is reached. Under favorable (warm) conditions, the harvest can take place every eight years, in [[North Africa]] every seven years. A cork oak can be harvested five to seventeen times in total.<ref name="Amorim" /> In order to minimize the damage to the trunk surface, harvesting can be carried out every three years, whereby only a third of the usable surface is removed. An important maintenance measure is [[pruning]], which begins around the age of ten at a height of about {{convert|3|m|abbr=on|frac=2}}. Some sources say an oak can provide around {{convert|100|to|200|kg|abbr=off}} of cork over its lifespan, and one hectare around {{convert|200|to|500|kg|abbr=on}} per year<ref name="page505">{{cite book |vauthors=Schütt et al. |title= Enzyklopädie der Laubbäume. Page 505}}</ref> while others suggest a single tree can produce on average {{convert|40|to|60|kg|abbr=on}} of cork per harvest,<ref name="Amorim" /> a comparatively higher value, as cork oaks can live more than 200 years in good conditions.<ref name=santos/><ref name="iucn status 19 November 2021" />

The cork is mainly used for the production of [[Bung (apparatus)|stoppers]] and [[wine cork|corks]], as well as for heat and sound insulation, cork
paper, badminton shuttlecocks, [[cricket ball]]s, handles of fishing rods and hand tools, special devices for the [[space industry]]<ref name='gil08'/> and for other technical applications (including [[composite material]]s, shoe soles, floor coverings).<ref name="page505" /><ref>{{cite web |last1=Pereira |date=2008 |first1=Alexandre |title=Biowerkstoff-Report |url=http://www.nova-institut.de/news-images/20081106-11/08-10+11+12_Biowerkstoff-Report.pdf |publisher=Nova Institute |page=28|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120118153342/http://www.nova-institut.de/news-images/20081106-11/08-10+11+12_Biowerkstoff-Report.pdf |archive-date=2012-01-18 }}</ref> Bottle cork production accounts for around 70% of the added value in cork cultivation. Since natural corks are increasingly being replaced by plastic or sheet metal closures, there could be a significant decline in the cork oak population in southwestern Europe, which endangers the biodiversity in these areas.<ref name="page505" />

The bark, which contains around twelve percent extractable [[tannin]], is also used. In addition, the acorns are used as feed in extensive pig fattening (acorn fattening), such as for [[Jamón ibérico|Iberian ham]] production;<ref>{{Cite web |title=Iberico ham from Spain |url=https://www.spain.info/en/discover-spain/iberian-ham/ |access-date=2023-12-30 |website=Spain.info |language=en}}</ref> although the holm oak (''[[Quercus ilex]]''), is preferred for this due to its sweeter fruits.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Holm oak, Gall oak and Cork oak - Monte Nevado |url=https://www.montenevado.com/en/content/holm-oak-gall-oak-and-cork-oak |access-date=2023-12-30 |website=www.montenevado.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=The pasture where we raise our 100% Iberian pigs {{!}} COVAP |url=https://www.ibericoscovap.com/en/meet-us/the-pastureland/ |access-date=2023-12-30 |website=www.ibericoscovap.com}}</ref> One cork oak tree can provide {{convert|15|to|30|kg|abbr=on}} of acorns per year.<ref name="page505" />

Cork oaks cannot legally be cut down in Portugal, except for [[forestry|forest management]] felling of old, unproductive trees, and, even in those cases, farmers need special permission from the Ministry of Agriculture.<ref>{{cite web |title=Decreto-Lei n.º 169/2001 |work=Diário da República Eletrónico |url=https://dre.pt/pesquisa/-/search/332749/details/maximized |publisher=[[Diário da República]] |access-date=31 December 2020}}</ref><ref name="iucn status 19 November 2021" />

Cork harvesting is done entirely without machinery, being dependent solely on human labour. Usually five people{{Citation needed|date=February 2021}} are required to harvest the tree's bark, using a small axe. The process mandates specialized training due to the skill required to harvest bark without inflicting too much damage to the tree.<ref>{{cite web |title=Cork harvesting |url=https://www.apcor.pt/en/cork/processing/cork-harvesting/ |publisher=APCOR |access-date=14 February 2021 |archive-date=4 March 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210304020928/https://www.apcor.pt/en/cork/processing/cork-harvesting/ }}</ref>

The European cork industry produces 300,000 [[tonne]]s of cork a year, with a value of [[Euro|€]]1.5 [[1000000000 (number)|billion]] and employing 30,000 people. [[Wine]] corks represent 15% of cork usage by weight but 66% of revenues.{{Citation needed|date=February 2021}}

Cork oaks are sometimes planted as individual trees, providing a minor income to their owners. The tree is also sometimes cultivated for ornament. [[Hybrid (biology)|Hybrids]] with Turkey oak (''[[Quercus cerris]]'') are not uncommon, both where their ranges overlap in the wild in southwest Europe and in cultivation; the hybrid ''Quercus'' × ''hispanica'' is known as Lucombe oak, for [[William Lucombe]], who first identified it.<ref>{{cite web |title=Lucombe Oak |url=https://www.keele.ac.uk/arboretum/ourtrees/speciesaccounts/lucombeoak/ |website=Keele University |access-date=8 October 2023 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |chapter=QUERCUS LUCOMBEANA, LUCOMBE OAK |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/trees-of-great-britain-and-ireland/quercus-lucombeana-lucombe-oak/4860387BC981AC8C72C0C8BD3F3ABE5E |title=The Trees of Great Britain and Ireland |publisher=Cambridge University Press |access-date=8 October 2023 |pages=1259–1267 |date=2014|doi=10.1017/CBO9781107252820.086 |isbn=978-1-107-25282-0 }}</ref>

Some cork is also produced in eastern [[Asia]] from the related Chinese cork oak (''[[Quercus variabilis]]'').{{Citation needed|date=February 2021}}

==Culture==
[[File:2018 winner ¨Whistler Cork Oak¨, Portugal.jpg|thumb|'The Whistler Tree', the world's largest cork tree]]

The cork oak is featured in the city arms of several cities in Portugal, such as the city of [[Reguengos de Monsaraz]], which shows a freshly harvested cork tree.<ref>{{cite web |title=Ordenação Heráldica de Reguengos de Monsaraz |url=http://arquivo.cm-reguengos-monsaraz.pt/pt/conteudos/o+concelho/heraldica/?redirectUrl=http://arquivo.cm-reguengos-monsaraz.pt/Portal.Municipios/SSO/Auth.aspx&originalUrl=http://arquivo.cm-reguengos-monsaraz.pt/pt/conteudos/o+concelho/heraldica/heraldica+da+camara+municipal+de+reguengos+de+mon.htm&logoffUrl=http://arquivo.cm-reguengos-monsaraz.pt/Portal.Municipios/SSO/AuthLogoff.aspx |publisher=Reguengos de Monsaraz Municipality |access-date=13 February 2021 }}{{Dead link|date=July 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

In 2007, a [[2 euro commemorative coin]] with the motif of a cork oak was issued in Portugal in memory of the Portuguese Presidency of the European Union.<ref>{{cite web |title=€2 commemorative coins - 2007 |url=https://www.ecb.europa.eu/euro/coins/comm/html/comm_2007.en.html |publisher=ecb.europa.eu |access-date=13 February 2021}}</ref>

=== Notable trees ===
In the Portuguese town of [[Águas de Moura]] lies the [[Sobreiro Monumental]] ('Monumental Cork Oak'), also known as 'The Whistler Tree', a tree 236 years old (planted in 1783/1784), over {{convert|14|m}} tall and with a trunk that requires at least three people to embrace it. It has been considered a National Monument since 1988, and [[Guinness World Records]] lists it as the largest cork tree in the world.<ref>{{cite web |title=Which is the largest and oldest cork oak in the world? |url=https://www.amorim.com/en/why-cork/myths-and-facts/Which-is-the-largest-and-oldest-cork-oak-in-the-world/110/401/#collapse401 |publisher=amorim.com |access-date=31 October 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=The World's Oldest, Largest Cork Tree – The Whistler Tree |date=3 April 2014 |url=https://vinepair.com/wine-blog/worlds-oldest-largest-cork-tree-the-whistler-tree/ |publisher=vinepair.com |access-date=31 October 2020}}</ref>

==== Cork oaks of California ====
[[File:Cork Oak Way.jpg|thumb|Cork Oak street sign]]
While native to the Mediterranean, cork oaks have been planted across several U.S. states with warm, mild climates, particularly in California. One of the oldest recorded cork oaks in the state, was planted in 1858, by Mexican miners, in the town of [[Campo Seco, California|Campo Seco]] in the Central Valley.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2013-07-16 |title=Campo Seco - myMotherLode.com |url=https://mymotherlode.com/community/guide/calaveras/campo-seco |access-date=2026-03-23 |language=en-US}}</ref> Another historic cork oak is in [[Napa, California|Napa]] and stands 89 feet tall with a 20 ft circumference.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Local Trees: The Cork Oak {{!}} The Real Dirt |url=https://ucanr.edu/blog/real-dirt/article/local-trees-cork-oak |access-date=2026-03-23 |website=ucanr.edu |language=en}}</ref> There are several streets or lanes in California with the name 'Cork Oak'. A street in Palo Alto, named 'Cork Oak Way' was established in 1960, in an area densely populated with cork oaks. {{As of|2026}}, eleven of these trees still lined this street.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Streets of Palo Alto |url=https://www.pastheritage.org/HousePixLists/PixListC.html#cork}}</ref>

=== Cork industry during World War II ===
By 1940, the United States imported nearly half the world’s cork production, for making everything from bottle caps to parts for military equipment. When Nazi Germany blockaded all Atlantic trade and cut off cork imports from Europe, the shortage was deemed a threat to U.S. national security. To address this threat, individuals such as Charles McManus Sr, CEO of Crown Cork and Seal and Woodbridge Metcalf, a Forestry Professor, participated in a national project to map and cultivate the domestic growth of cork oaks. As a result, a military transport plane delivered a load of cork oak acorns from Morocco to the US. Throughout this project, over five hundred cork oaks were planted in the University of California at Davis.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Taylor |first=David A. |title=Cork wars: intrigue and industry in World War II |date=2018 |publisher=Johns Hopkins University Press |isbn=978-1-4214-2691-4 |location=Baltimore, Maryland}}</ref> {{clear}}
